title: The Nazis in Power
description: How Hitler turned Germany into a dictatorship in 1933–34, and how the Nazi state controlled ordinary life through terror, propaganda, youth movements and persecution.

notes.heading: From Democracy to Dictatorship, 1933–34
notes.body: Hitler became Chancellor in January 1933, but within eighteen months he had destroyed German democracy. In February 1933 the Reichstag (parliament) building burned down. The Nazis blamed a Communist plot and persuaded President Hindenburg to sign the Reichstag Fire Decree, which suspended civil rights and let them arrest thousands of opponents. In March 1933 the Enabling Act allowed Hitler to make laws without the Reichstag for four years — this was the legal foundation of the dictatorship. Trade unions were banned in May, and by July 1933 all other political parties were banned: Germany was a one-party state. In June 1934 came the Night of the Long Knives: Hitler ordered the murder of Ernst Röhm and the leadership of the SA, whose wild violence frightened the army, along with other old enemies. The army, grateful, swore an oath of personal loyalty to Hitler. When Hindenburg died in August 1934, Hitler merged the offices of president and chancellor and took the title Führer (leader). No election, no revolution — step by step, using law, fear and violence, Germany had become a dictatorship.

notes.heading: The Police State: Terror and Fear
notes.body: Nazi Germany was a police state — people were controlled by fear as much as by enthusiasm. The SS, led by Heinrich Himmler, grew from Hitler's bodyguard into the vast organisation responsible for terror and, later, for running the camp system. The Gestapo was the secret state police: it could arrest and imprison people without trial, tapped telephones and opened letters, and relied heavily on informers — neighbours, colleagues and even children denouncing each other. People who spoke out, listened to foreign radio or told jokes about the regime could disappear into concentration camps. The first camp, Dachau, opened in March 1933 for political prisoners such as Communists and trade unionists; the system later expanded enormously. Judges, lawyers and the courts were brought under Nazi control, so the terror appeared legal. Because nobody knew who might be an informer, most people kept quiet — fear of the knock on the door did the Gestapo's work for it.

notes.heading: Propaganda and Censorship
notes.body: If terror frightened Germans, propaganda tried to win their hearts. Joseph Goebbels ran the Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda, controlling newspapers, radio, film and the arts. Cheap radios (the 'People's Receiver') were mass-produced so that Hitler's speeches reached every home — though tuning into foreign stations became a crime. Radios and loudspeakers blared in factories and town squares. Huge events like the annual Nuremberg rallies, with their torches, banners and massed crowds, made individuals feel part of something unstoppable. The 1936 Berlin Olympics were staged as a giant showcase of a 'new Germany'. Censorship was the other side of the coin: no newspaper could print anything critical, and in May 1933 students burned thousands of books by Jewish and anti-Nazi authors in public bonfires. Art, music and film had to glorify Nazi ideals. The message everywhere was simple and repeated: Hitler is always right, Germany is strong, and the Nazis have saved the nation.

notes.heading: Youth and Women in Nazi Germany
notes.body: The Nazis wanted to shape the next generation completely. In school, subjects were twisted to fit Nazi ideas: history glorified Germany's past, biology taught false racial theories, and PE took up more timetable time to build strong soldiers and mothers. Teachers had to join a Nazi organisation. Outside school, boys joined the Hitler Youth, learning marching, camping and military skills; girls joined the League of German Maidens, learning fitness and homemaking. From 1936 membership was effectively compulsory. Many young people enjoyed the activities and friendships; others resented the pressure, and small rebel groups like the Edelweiss Pirates showed that not all youth was won over. For women, Nazi policy was summed up by the slogan 'Kinder, Küche, Kirche' (children, kitchen, church). Women were pushed out of professional jobs, encouraged to marry and have large families with loans and medals for mothers, and expected to stay at home — until, ironically, the coming war forced women back into factories from the late 1930s.

notes.heading: The Nazis and the Churches
notes.body: Christianity was a problem for the Nazis: they wanted total loyalty, but millions of Germans gave their deepest loyalty to God. Hitler at first made deals. In 1933 he signed a Concordat (agreement) with the Catholic Church: the Church stayed out of politics, and in return the Nazis promised not to interfere with it — a promise they soon broke, closing Catholic schools and youth groups and arresting critical priests. Among Protestants, the Nazis created an official 'Reich Church' that mixed Christian symbols with Nazi ideology. Some Christians resisted. Pastor Martin Niemöller helped found the Confessing Church, which rejected Nazi control; he was sent to a concentration camp. Dietrich Bonhoeffer, a Lutheran pastor, spoke out against the regime and was eventually executed for his opposition. Most church leaders, however, chose quiet compromise rather than open defiance, which raises the question historians still debate: were the churches opponents of the regime, or bystanders who looked away?

notes.heading: Persecution of Minorities
notes.body: From the very start, the Nazi regime persecuted groups it falsely labelled enemies or 'inferior'. Jewish Germans were the main target of a steady, legalised hatred: in April 1933 a boycott of Jewish shops began; Jewish people were dismissed from government jobs; and in 1935 the Nuremberg Laws stripped them of German citizenship and banned marriages between Jews and other Germans. In November 1938 came Kristallnacht (the 'Night of Broken Glass'), a nationwide, organised attack in which Jewish shops, homes and synagogues were smashed and burned, thousands of men were arrested, and nearly 100 people were killed. Jewish families lost their livelihoods, their rights and their dignity, and tens of thousands emigrated while they still could. Other groups also suffered: Roma (Gypsy) people were persecuted; Black Germans faced discrimination; people with disabilities were forcibly sterilised and later murdered; gay men and political opponents were imprisoned. This escalating persecution was the road that led, during the Second World War, to the Holocaust.

notes.heading: The Economy: Jobs, Public Works and Rearmament
notes.body: The Nazis claimed credit for a 'German economic miracle'. Unemployment, over 6 million when Hitler took power, fell sharply — officially to almost zero by 1939. How? Huge public works programmes, most famously the autobahns (motorways), put hundreds of thousands to work. Conscription reintroduced in 1935 absorbed young men into a growing army. Most importantly, rearmament — secretly at first, then openly — created millions of jobs in weapons factories, steel and chemicals. The 'Beauty of Labour' and 'Strength Through Joy' organisations offered workers better conditions, leisure activities and cheap holidays to win their loyalty. But the statistics flattered the regime: women and Jewish people forced out of jobs were not counted, and wages stayed low while living costs rose. Ordinary Germans ate less butter so the economy could make more guns — 'guns before butter' was the real policy. Still, for families that had suffered the despair of the Depression, having work again felt like salvation, and many gave Hitler the credit. This apparent success is a key reason why opposition within Germany stayed small.

flashcards.definition: The emergency decree of February 1933, issued after the parliament building burned down, which suspended civil rights and allowed mass arrests of Nazi opponents.
flashcards.example: Thousands of Communists were arrested within days, clearing the way for the Enabling Act.

flashcards.definition: The law that let Hitler make laws for four years without the Reichstag. It was the legal foundation of the Nazi dictatorship.
flashcards.example: After it passed, other parties and trade unions were quickly banned.

flashcards.definition: The purge of June 1934 in which Hitler had SA leader Ernst Röhm and other rivals murdered, winning the loyalty of the army.
flashcards.example: Afterwards, soldiers swore an oath of personal loyalty to Hitler rather than to Germany.

flashcards.definition: The Nazi secret state police, which could arrest and imprison people without trial and relied heavily on informers and denunciations.
flashcards.example: A neighbour could report someone for listening to foreign radio or criticising Hitler.

flashcards.definition: The elite Nazi organisation led by Heinrich Himmler, originally Hitler's bodyguard, which grew to run the police state and the concentration camp system.
flashcards.example: The SS ran Dachau, the first concentration camp, opened in March 1933 for political prisoners.

flashcards.definition: A prison camp where the Nazis held political opponents and persecuted groups without trial, under brutal conditions. The first was Dachau (1933).
flashcards.example: Communists, trade unionists and later Jewish people, Roma and others were imprisoned in camps.

flashcards.definition: The Nazi youth organisation for boys, teaching military skills, fitness and Nazi ideology; girls joined the League of German Maidens. Membership was effectively compulsory from 1936.
flashcards.example: Some teenagers rebelled instead, joining groups like the Edelweiss Pirates.

flashcards.definition: Meaning 'children, kitchen, church' — the Nazi slogan summing up the role expected of women: homemaking and raising large families rather than careers.
flashcards.example: Women were given marriage loans and medals for having many children.

flashcards.definition: Laws that stripped Jewish Germans of citizenship and banned marriage between Jews and other Germans — a key step in legalising antisemitic persecution.
flashcards.example: The laws defined who counted as Jewish by ancestry, not by belief.

flashcards.definition: The 'Night of Broken Glass', November 1938: an organised nationwide attack on Jewish shops, homes and synagogues; about 100 people were killed and 30,000 Jewish men sent to camps.
flashcards.example: After Kristallnacht, tens of thousands of Jewish families tried desperately to emigrate.

flashcards.definition: The Nazi idea of a 'people's community' — a racially defined national family with no class divisions, from which Jews, Roma and other targeted groups were excluded.
flashcards.example: Propaganda showed workers, farmers and soldiers united behind the Führer as one community.

flashcards.definition: The motorways built as part of Nazi public works programmes, which — along with rearmament and conscription — cut official unemployment almost to zero by 1939.
flashcards.example: The jobs figures were flattered: women and Jewish people pushed out of work were not counted.

questions.stem: Which law, passed in March 1933, allowed Hitler to make laws without the Reichstag?
choices: The Nuremberg Laws
The Enabling Act
The Reichstag Fire Decree
The Treaty of Versailles
questions.explanation: The Enabling Act (March 1933) gave Hitler the power to pass laws without parliament for four years. It was the legal foundation of the dictatorship; the Nuremberg Laws came in 1935.

questions.stem: Who was the head of the SS?
choices: Joseph Goebbels
Ernst Röhm
Heinrich Himmler
Hermann Goering
questions.explanation: Heinrich Himmler led the SS, which ran the police state and the camp system. Goebbels ran propaganda, and Röhm led the SA until he was killed in 1934.

questions.stem: Why did Hitler order the Night of the Long Knives in June 1934?
choices: To defeat the British army
To remove Ernst Röhm and the SA leadership, whose violence threatened his alliance with the army
To punish the Reichstag for refusing to pass laws
To stop the persecution of Jewish people
questions.explanation: Röhm's SA wanted a bigger role and alarmed the regular army. By murdering Röhm and other SA leaders, Hitler secured the army's loyalty — soldiers then swore a personal oath to him.

questions.stem: What happened in August 1934 that completed Hitler's control of Germany?
choices: The Enabling Act was passed
The Reichstag burned down
President Hindenburg died and Hitler combined the roles of president and chancellor, taking the title Führer
Germany invaded Poland
questions.explanation: When Hindenburg died in August 1934, Hitler merged the offices of president and chancellor and became Führer. With the army already sworn to him personally, no institution could now remove him.

questions.stem: Why was the Gestapo so effective despite being relatively small?
choices: It had the largest budget in Europe
It relied on informers, so ordinary people feared that neighbours, colleagues or even children might denounce them
It controlled the German army
It only operated in Berlin
questions.explanation: The Gestapo depended on denunciations from the public. Because nobody could be sure who was an informer, people policed themselves — fear did much of the Gestapo's work.

questions.stem: How did Goebbels use radio to spread Nazi propaganda?
choices: He banned all radios in Germany
Cheap 'People's Receivers' were mass-produced so Hitler's speeches reached every home, while listening to foreign stations became a crime
Radios could only play classical music
He allowed every party equal time on air
questions.explanation: Mass-producing cheap radios put Nazi broadcasts in almost every home and workplace. At the same time, tuning into foreign broadcasts was criminalised, so Germans heard only the regime's message.

questions.stem: Which group showed that not all young Germans accepted Nazi control of youth?
choices: The Hitler Youth
The League of German Maidens
The Edelweiss Pirates
The SS
questions.explanation: The Edelweiss Pirates were loose groups of working-class teenagers who avoided the Hitler Youth, wore their own clothes and sometimes fought with Hitler Youth patrols — proof that control of the young was never total.

questions.stem: What was the main aim of Nazi policy towards women, summed up by 'Kinder, Küche, Kirche'?
choices: To recruit women into the army
To encourage women to leave professional jobs, marry and raise large families
To give women the vote
To send women to university in greater numbers
questions.explanation: The slogan means 'children, kitchen, church'. Women were pushed out of professions and rewarded with loans and medals for motherhood — until wartime labour shortages forced women back into factories.

questions.stem: Which of these best describes Nazi policy towards the churches?
choices: The Nazis immediately banned all religion in 1933
Hitler made deals such as the Catholic Concordat, broke them when convenient, and created an official Reich Church, while some pastors like Niemöller and Bonhoeffer resisted
All churches enthusiastically supported every Nazi policy
The churches were left completely alone throughout the period
questions.explanation: Policy was a mix of deal-making and pressure: the 1933 Concordat was soon broken, Protestants were herded into a Nazi Reich Church, and resisters like Niemöller and Bonhoeffer were imprisoned.

questions.stem: What were the Nuremberg Laws of 1935?
choices: Laws that banned other political parties
Laws that stripped Jewish Germans of citizenship and banned marriage between Jews and other Germans
Laws that created the Hitler Youth
Laws that ended reparation payments
questions.explanation: The Nuremberg Laws turned antisemitism into law: Jews lost German citizenship and could not marry non-Jews. They were a milestone on the road from discrimination to genocide.

questions.stem: A German worker in 1937 has a job on an autobahn and enjoys a cheap 'Strength Through Joy' holiday. What would a historian remind us before calling this an 'economic miracle'?
choices: That public works were actually banned by the Nazis
That unemployment figures were flattered because women and Jewish people pushed out of work were not counted, and the boom rested on rearmament, not rising living standards
That the autobahns were never finished
That all German workers were paid in food rather than money
questions.explanation: The recovery was real but skewed: the statistics excluded persecuted groups and women, wages stayed low, and the boom was built on weapons production — 'guns before butter'.

choices: A Nazi party rally held each year in Nuremberg
The burning of the Reichstag building
An organised nationwide attack on Jewish shops, homes and synagogues in November 1938
The opening of the first concentration camp
questions.explanation: Kristallnacht (9–10 November 1938) was a coordinated pogrom: synagogues were burned, Jewish businesses smashed, about 100 people killed and 30,000 Jewish men sent to camps.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why opposition inside Nazi Germany remained small?
choices: Everyone in Germany fully agreed with every Nazi policy
A combination of terror (Gestapo, camps), propaganda, economic recovery and genuine popularity for some policies made open resistance extremely dangerous and rare
The Allies refused to help German opponents
Germany had no traditions of political opposition
questions.explanation: Opposition was squeezed from both sides: fear of arrest and the camps silenced critics, while propaganda, falling unemployment and popular foreign-policy successes won real support for the regime.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly shows the escalation of persecution of Jewish Germans?
choices: Nuremberg Laws → Kristallnacht → boycott of Jewish shops
Kristallnacht → boycott of Jewish shops → Nuremberg Laws
Boycott of Jewish shops (1933) → Nuremberg Laws (1935) → Kristallnacht (1938)
Boycott of Jewish shops → Kristallnacht → Nuremberg Laws
questions.explanation: Persecution escalated step by step: the shop boycott of April 1933, the citizenship-stripping Nuremberg Laws of 1935, and the violent nationwide Kristallnacht pogrom of November 1938.

questions.stem: How was school education changed under the Nazis?
choices: Subjects were rewritten to promote Nazi ideas — history glorified Germany, biology taught racial theories, and PE time increased
All schools were closed so children could work in factories
Children were encouraged to question all authority
Religious education was made compulsory for everyone
questions.explanation: Education became indoctrination: textbooks were rewritten, teachers joined a Nazi organisation, and subjects from history to biology served the regime's ideology, while extra PE prepared boys for war and girls for motherhood.
